strengths: The paper is clearly structured and tackles an important challenge in vision architectures: balancing computational efficiency, local focusing, and global receptive fields.

The proposed SEMA mechanism (window attention + positional bias + sequence-level average pooling) is conceptually simple, lightweight, and straightforward to implement without requiring complex scan operations.
Empirical evaluation shows competitive results for a tiny model (~26M parameters) on ImageNet-1K classification (83.7% top-1) and COCO object detection/segmentation.
weaknesses: Disconnect between theoretical motivation and proposed method: The proof that attention weights disperse as $\Theta(1/n)$ relies on bounded inputs and essentially adapts existing results (e.g., Veličković et al., 2024). More importantly, the fact that attention weights decay as $O(1/n)$ does not justify replacing input-dependent global attention with uniform, unweighted arithmetic averaging ($ rac{1}{n}\sum v_j$). Doing so completely discards content-based global selection.

Misleading nomenclature and limited architectural novelty: Despite being branded as 'Mamba-like Attention (SEMA)', the proposed block contains neither state-space models, recurrence, nor selective scans. It is essentially standard windowed softmax attention combined with LePE and global average pooling, inserted into the macro-architecture of MILA (Han et al., 2024).

Limited evaluation scale: All experiments are restricted to a single model capacity (Tiny, ~26M parameters). There are no experiments on Small, Base, or Large model variants, leaving the scalability claims across model capacities unsupported.

Marginal gains and weak ablation studies: The core component of the paper—the arithmetic averaging term—provides only a +0.2% improvement on ImageNet-1K (Table 5, 83.5% vs. 83.7%). There are no standard deviations or multiple random seeds reported to verify whether this difference is statistically significant.

Incomplete comparison at higher resolutions: In Table 3, SEMA is compared exclusively against VMamba-T, omitting direct comparisons with MILA-T or other window-based baselines (e.g., Swin) at larger resolutions ($384^2, 672^2, 768^2$).
Typographical error in training setup: In Section 5, the text states 'The initial learning rate is set to $4 \times 10^3$', which is clearly an erroneous exponent.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and active problem in vision architectures: mitigating the quadratic complexity of global self-attention while maintaining long-range context and local focusing.
The manuscript is organized clearly, with straightforward algorithmic descriptions (Algorithms 1 and 2) and informative architectural diagrams (Figures 3 and 4).

Empirical evaluation includes standardized benchmarks (ImageNet-1K classification, multi-resolution finetuning, and COCO object detection/instance segmentation) benchmarked against a wide range of CNN, Transformer, and SSM baselines.
weaknesses: Theoretical justification is mathematically trivial and conceptually flawed: Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 merely re-state that any continuous positive function on a compact set attains a strictly positive minimum and finite maximum, so normalization by a sum of $n$ elements naturally scales as $\Theta(1/n)$. Because attention weights must sum to 1, their mean must be $1/n$; this does not imply that attention weights become uniform or content-agnostic. The ratio $\phi(b)/\phi(a)$ can be arbitrarily large (e.g., $e^{\Delta z}$ in softmax), preserving extreme selectivity. Concluding that this dispersion justifies replacing global attention with an unweighted arithmetic average ($\frac{1}{n}\sum v_j$) is a non-sequitur.

The architectural novelty is minimal and the naming is misleading: The method simply adds a broadcasted global average pooling of values $V$ to local window attention within the MILA macro-block. SEMA contains no state space model, no selective scan, no recurrence, and no causal gating; designating window attention plus global pooling as 'Mamba-like Attention' is a misnomer.

Empirical improvements are marginal and lack statistical significance: On ImageNet-1K, SEMA-T achieves 83.7% vs. MILA-T's reported 83.5% (+0.2%). The ablation in Table 5 indicates that the proposed homogeneous mixing contributes only 0.2% top-1 accuracy. Without multi-seed runs, standard deviations, or significance testing, this difference is within standard training noise.

Evaluation scope is limited to Tiny models: Experiments are conducted only at the ~26M parameter scale. No Small, Base, or Large configurations are evaluated to confirm scalability across model capacities.

Absence of actual latency and throughput benchmarks: Despite the paper explicitly motivating the architecture for efficient edge deployment, no real-world runtime metrics (e.g., FPS, latency on GPU/edge hardware) are reported, relying solely on theoretical FLOPs.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: balancing local focus and global context in efficient vision backbones with linear computational scaling in image size.
The proposed module is simple and straightforward to implement, combining local windowed softmax attention with an unweighted global average pooling term.
The model achieves competitive results within its parameter class (~26M parameters) on ImageNet-1K (83.7% top-1) and COCO detection/instance segmentation compared to MILA-T.
weaknesses: Misleading terminology and conceptual disconnect: Calling the proposed mechanism 'Mamba-like Attention' is inaccurate. SEMA replaces linear attention / selective state-space mechanisms entirely with standard local windowed softmax attention and a global average pooling vector. Truncating context via local windows is the hallmark of windowed transformers (e.g., Swin), not state-space models. Inserting this into the macro-architecture of MILA does not make the attention mechanism itself 'Mamba-like'.

Triviality and questionable motivation of theoretical results: Lemma 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 state that if logits are bounded on a compact domain, any continuous normalization $\Phi$ scales as $\Theta(1/n)$. This is an elementary property of normalizing $n$ positive terms bounded in $[c_1, c_2]$ and largely mirrors Theorem 2.2 of Veličković et al. (2024). Furthermore, dispersion is widely understood as a pathological degradation of attention selectivity; framing uniform global average pooling as a theoretically motivated approximation to 'embrace' dispersion is an unconvincing post-hoc justification for adding a standard global pooling residual.

Incomplete empirical evaluation and missing baselines: The evaluation is restricted entirely to tiny models (~26M parameters), leaving the scalability to Small, Base, or Large models untested. In Table 3 (high-resolution finetuning), the primary baseline MILA-T is notably absent, and only VMamba is reported. In Table 4 (COCO 1x), SEMA underperforms VMamba-T in both bounding box and mask AP (47.2 vs 47.3 APb, 42.4 vs 42.7 APm).

Lack of wall-clock efficiency benchmarks: Although the paper repeatedly claims efficiency and suitability for edge deployment, no throughput (images/sec), latency, or peak GPU memory measurements are reported. FLOPs alone are known to correlate poorly with runtime for windowed operations and state-space models.

Superficial ablation study: The ablation section (Table 5) consists of only a single data point comparing SEMA with and without the global averaging term (+0.2% on ImageNet). There is no analysis of window sizes, positional encodings (RoPE vs. LePE), or comparisons against established lightweight global pooling/mixing alternatives (e.g., global depthwise convolution, SENet-style excitation, or shifted windows).

strengths: The paper evaluates the proposed model across several standard computer vision benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K classification at standard (224x224) and large resolutions (up to 1024x1024), COCO object detection/instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation.
The proposed SEMA module is computationally lightweight and straightforward to implement, achieving faster inference times than MILA at high image resolutions while maintaining competitive accuracy.
The generalized attention formulation provides a unified framework to analyze dispersion bounds across softmax, linear, and differential attention variants.
weaknesses: Disconnection between theoretical dispersion and the proposed arithmetic averaging: Theorem 3.3 proves that individual attention weights decay as O(1/n) on compact domains, but vanishing weights do not imply convergence to a uniform distribution or justify approximating attention with an unweighted arithmetic average (1/n sum v_j). Because the dispersion coefficient phi(b)/phi(a) can be as large as 10^5 to 10^6 (as noted in Section 3.1), attention weights can remain highly non-uniform. Equating dispersion with unweighted averaging is a conceptual overreach.

Questionable architectural framing: SEMA contains neither state-space formulations, selective scanning, nor recurrence. It computes standard windowed softmax attention, adds a global average of V, and applies depthwise convolution (LePE) within the MILA macro-block. Terming this mechanism 'Mamba-like Attention' is misleading and obscures the fact that it is a window transformer with global average pooling.

Limited architectural novelty and marginal contribution of averaging: Combining local window attention with global pooling or downsampled global tokens is an established concept in vision transformers (e.g., Twins, Focal Transformer). Ablation Table 7 indicates that adding the value projection alone accounts for most of the performance gain (+0.6%), while the global averaging component contributes only +0.2% on standard ImageNet-1K.

Incomplete high-resolution baselines: In Table 3, the multi-resolution scaling experiments only compare SEMA against VMamba-T. Standard hierarchical vision transformer baselines designed for variable resolutions, such as Swin Transformer or CSwin, are omitted from this evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: the trade-off between computational efficiency, receptive field size, and token dispersion in vision transformers and state-space architectures.

Comprehensive empirical benchmarking across several standard vision benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K at multiple resolutions (224x224 up to 1024x1024), object detection/instance segmentation on COCO, and semantic segmentation on ADE20K.
The proposed formulation demonstrates practical inference speed advantages over linear-attention baselines like MILA at large image resolutions (Table 4).
weaknesses: Conceptual gap in theoretical motivation: The paper proves that Φ-normalized attention weights are bounded by O(1/n) on compact sets (Theorem 3.3). However, an O(1/n) upper bound on attention weights does not imply that attention weights converge to a uniform distribution (1/n). Inferring that attention inevitably behaves as uniform arithmetic averaging (1/n sum v_j) is mathematically unsupported, making the theoretical justification for the proposed method fundamentally flawed.

The theoretical contribution itself is marginal: Bounding phi(x_i) / sum_j phi(x_j) by [phi(a)/(n phi(b)), phi(b)/(n phi(a))] for continuous, strictly positive phi on a compact set is an immediate application of the Extreme Value Theorem, offering minimal theoretical depth beyond existing dispersion analyses such as Veličković et al. (2025).

Misleading framing and terminology: The paper frames the method as 'Mamba like Attention' (SEMA). However, as shown in Equation (12) and Algorithm 1, the proposed module consists simply of standard Window Softmax Attention + LePE + sequence-wide Global Average Pooling of V. It contains no state-space modeling, no recurrence, and no selective scanning. Simply placing window attention into a macro-block previously used by Mamba/MILA does not justify branding the attention operator as 'Mamba-like'.

Marginal empirical impact of the core contribution: Table 7 shows that at standard 224x224 resolution, adding the global averaging component yields only a +0.2% gain (83.5% to 83.7%), while adding the value linear projection accounts for the majority of the gain (+0.6%, from 82.9% to 83.5%). The paper's performance advantage over MILA appears largely driven by added parameters (value projection) rather than the proposed dispersion-mitigation mechanism.

Lack of contextualization and comparison with prior local-global architectures: Combining local/window attention with global pooling or coarse global representations is a well-established concept in vision architectures (e.g., MixFormer, CoatNet, Focal Transformer). The paper does not sufficiently discuss or benchmark against these closely related hybrid designs.

Presentation and writing issues: The manuscript contains multiple typographical and grammatical errors (e.g., 'it is not casual' instead of 'causal' in Section 3.3, 'medicals image segmentation tasks', and ungrammatical phrasing in Section 6).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely challenge: reducing the computational cost of visual attention mechanisms while preserving global context and scaling effectively to large image resolutions.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across standard vision benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K classification, high-resolution ImageNet scaling (up to 1024x1024), MS-COCO object detection/instance segmentation, and ADE20K semantic segmentation.

Strong inference speedups: by replacing linear attention in MILA with windowed attention and a global average pooling branch, SEMA achieves substantial latency reductions at large image resolutions (e.g., ~33% faster than MILA at 1024x1024 and 2048x2048 resolutions).
Helpful ablation studies dissecting the impact of the value projection and the uniform averaging term across different image resolutions.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty and depth: Theorem 3.3 relies on the standard extreme value theorem—continuous functions on compact sets attain their minimum and maximum, meaning logits are bounded in a compact interval [-M, M], from which the normalized attention weights are trivially upper-bounded by O(1/n). This is essentially an extension of existing observations (e.g., Veličković et al., 2025) and does not provide profound new theoretical insights into attention behavior.

Conceptual leap from dispersion to uniform averaging: While the upper bound on attention coefficients decays as O(1/n) when n grows large under compact inputs, equating or approximating full softmax attention with an unweighted arithmetic average of value tokens (1/n sum v_j) is an unsubstantiated heuristic leap. Attention's selective, input-dependent routing cannot be fundamentally substituted by uniform global average pooling, and justifying uniform average pooling through this theoretical lens remains tenuous.

Misleading nomenclature: Despite the title referring to 'Mamba like Attention', the proposed attention block (Equation 12, Algorithm 1) consists entirely of windowed softmax attention, LePE, RoPE, and global average pooling of values. It contains no state-space equations, selective scanning, or recurrent mechanism. Placing window attention inside the macro-architecture previously used by MILA does not make the attention mechanism itself Mamba-like.

Crucial missing baseline in high-resolution experiments: In Table 3, SEMA is only compared against VMamba-T across larger image resolutions (384^2 to 1024^2), but entirely omits MILA-T—the exact model architecture upon which SEMA is built. Without comparing against MILA-T on these high-resolution evaluations, it is impossible to disentangle whether the gains over VMamba stem from the proposed window+averaging mechanism or were already present in the MILA macro-design.

Confounding parameter capacity in standard benchmarks: In Table 7, the ablation at 224x224 shows that adding a linear value projection accounts for +0.6% of the accuracy gain, whereas the averaging term accounts for only +0.2%. Because MILA did not use a value projection, much of the reported performance advantage of SEMA over MILA in Table 2 is attributable to the extra parameters from the value projection rather than the architectural concept.

Minor presentation issues: In-text citation formatting glitches (e.g., 'Wu & et al, 2024' instead of proper et al. formatting) and referencing a concurrent/future citation ('Dayag et al., 2026') as external validation in the main text.
